errors.quote: has a fractional part and is only stored approximately
errors.problem: This is stated for all floats, including the example 3.0. But 3.0 is stored exactly, and so are 0.5 and 0.25, as the lesson itself says later ("0.5 is exact"). The opening sentence contradicts the lesson's own honest-scope point that the problem is not 'all floats are wrong'.
errors.fix: Say that a float can hold a fractional part and that many such values (like 0.1) can only be stored approximately, while others (3.0, 0.5, 0.25) are stored exactly. Tell the learner the lesson will show which are which.

errors.quote: This is documented behaviour and you can read it in `help(round)`.
errors.problem: The docstring that help(round) shows does not mention ties going to the even number. It only says that round rounds to a given precision and that it returns an int when ndigits is omitted. A learner who checks there will find nothing to back up the claim.
errors.fix: Point to the round() entry on the Built-in Functions page of the Python documentation. It states that when two multiples are equally close, rounding goes to the even choice, and it has a note explaining the round(2.675, 2) case.

errors.quote: `math.fsum` sums more accurately than a plain `sum`.
errors.problem: As far as I recall, the built-in sum() has used compensated (Neumaier) summation for floats since Python 3.12. That is why the run printed 1.0 for sum([0.1] * 10). So calling it a 'plain sum' is wrong for current Python, and the note 'math.fsum sums more accurately than sum' gives a misleading picture. fsum is still correctly rounded and can beat sum in hard cases, but this example does not show any difference.
errors.fix: Scope the claim: in Python 3.12 and later, sum() of floats already compensates for rounding error, and math.fsum gives the correctly rounded result. Tell the learner to check this in 'What's New in Python 3.12' and the math.fsum docs. Show the difference with the explicit loop from the lesson (total += 0.1 ten times gives 0.9999999999999999) against math.fsum([0.1] * 10), which gives 1.0. Add import math to the extension session. Correct the note to match.

improvements.quote: The exact sum falls between two neighbouring floats, and the result is the upper one
improvements.problem: The lesson doesn't explain why the result is the upper float, so the learner can't rebuild this step. The exact sum of the stored 0.1 and the stored 0.2 lies exactly halfway between the stored 0.3 and the next float up. The tie goes to the float whose last bit is 0, which here is the upper one.
improvements.fix: Add one or two sentences: Python rounds each exact result to the nearest float. Here the exact sum is exactly halfway between two floats, and ties go to the 'even' one (last binary digit 0), which happens to be the upper one. Link this to the same round-half-to-even rule the learner meets later with round(2.5).

improvements.quote: When one value is 0, "a billionth of the bigger value" is a billionth of almost nothing
improvements.problem: This suggests the failure happens because 1e-12 is small. The real mechanism is stronger: with only a relative tolerance, no nonzero number is ever close to 0. The allowed gap is a billionth of the nonzero value, and the actual gap is the whole value. So math.isclose(1.0, 0.0) and math.isclose(1e-300, 0.0) are False too.
improvements.fix: State the general rule. With the default abs_tol=0.0, isclose(x, 0.0) is True only when x is exactly 0, because the difference |x| can never be at most 1e-9 times |x|. That is why abs_tol is needed whenever an expected value may be zero (for example a residual or an error that should vanish).

improvements.quote: it affects values that are not sums of powers of 2
improvements.problem: The scope is still a little too broad. A value is exact only if it is a sum of powers of 2 that fits in the 53 significant bits. And '== is fine ... for exactly representable values' only holds while the results of the arithmetic also fit. 2.0**53 + 1, shown in the extension, is a sum of powers of 2 and is still not stored exactly.
improvements.fix: Add 'that fit in 53 significant bits' and refer to the 2**53 example in the extension, so the rule the learner rebuilds has the right edges.
